question: What happens to my sleep if I stop screens before bed?

source.title: Screens before bed: what they cost your sleep
source.publisher: Test fixture written for this repo (numbers are illustrative)
quotes: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night.
In one study, each hour of screen use in the hour before bed was linked to about 20 minutes less sleep that night.
People who use screens in bed also take longer to fall asleep: around 15 minutes longer on average.
If you lose 30 minutes a night, by the end of a working week you are two and a half hours short.
It helps a little, but most of the effect comes from staying engaged, not from the light alone.
Putting the phone away is what makes the biggest difference.
Stop screens 30 to 60 minutes before bed.

explain.caption: What happens to your sleep when screens come to bed?
This is the last hour before you go to sleep.
Screens can fill some or all of that hour.
Screen time in that hour cuts your sleep that night.
Screens in bed also make you slower to fall asleep.
But dimming the screen barely helps. Putting it away does.
Sleep debt is sleep you needed but did not get.
Each short night adds to the debt.
So small losses each night add up over a working week.
Now make it yours. Answer a few questions.

compare.label: Screens until bed, phone in bed
Stop an hour before, phone outside

tradeoffs: Evening screens can be how you relax or keep in touch, but they cost some sleep that night.
Keeping the phone outside the bedroom removes the pull to check it, but you may need another alarm clock.
A paper book or calm audio can fill the wind-down time, but a new habit takes a while to settle.
leftOut: The 20 and 15 minute figures are averages from studies of groups; your own effect may be larger or smaller.
The model adds the two effects together; they may overlap, so the real total could be smaller.
A weekend lie-in pays back part of the debt, but the article gives no number, so the model leaves it out.
Night mode helps a little, but the article gives no number, so the model does not include it.
Stress, caffeine, noise and a regular bedtime also change sleep, and the model leaves them out.
